G1A.note: General class opens most of HF, but four bands are shared with Extra-only segments at the bottom: 80, 40, 20 and 15 metres. Learn where your segment starts on each. 60 metres is different again — five fixed channels, upper sideband, with a power limit referenced to an effective radiated power rather than output.
key_facts: Generals are excluded from parts of 80, 40, 20 and 15 m
A primary allocation takes precedence over a secondary user
60 m is channelised: five channels, USB, 100 W ERP
The whole emission must fall inside your privileges

G1B.note: PRB-1 requires local authorities to reasonably accommodate amateur antennas, but does not override every restriction. Beacons are limited to 100 W and must be under automatic, local or remote control. Broadcasting, business traffic and encoded messages remain prohibited, and one-way transmissions are only allowed in the listed exceptions.
key_facts: Beacon power limit is 100 W
Antenna structures over 200 ft or near airports need FAA/FCC notification
Only one beacon may be automatically controlled per band from a station
Good amateur practice is judged by the FCC

G1C.note: The power rule is simple to state and easy to get wrong: 1500 W PEP output, and always the minimum necessary. Some segments are lower — 200 W PEP on 30 m and in the Novice/Technician HF CW segments. Data emissions have a symbol-rate and bandwidth framework, and 60 m has its own effective-radiated-power ceiling.
key_facts: Maximum 1500 W PEP output, and only the minimum necessary
30 m is limited to 200 W PEP and no phone
60 m is limited to 100 W ERP relative to a half-wave dipole
Power is measured as peak envelope power at the transmitter output

G1D.note: The volunteer examiner system runs the exams. To be a VE you must hold General or higher — and to administer a particular element you must hold a class above it, so Extras are needed for the Extra exam. When you pass an upgrade you get a CSCE, and you may operate with your new privileges immediately by appending the correct identifier.
key_facts: Three accredited VEs are required to administer an exam
A VE must be accredited by a VEC and hold General or higher
After upgrading, identify with your call sign plus /AG or /AE until the licence appears
A CSCE is valid for 365 days for element credit

G1E.note: Control category determines who is responsible and where. Automatic control is restricted to specific station types; anything else needs a control operator at a control point. Third-party traffic across borders requires an agreement between the two countries. Automatically controlled digital stations may only operate in designated segments.
key_facts: Automatic control is limited to repeater, auxiliary, beacon and space stations
Third-party traffic abroad requires a third-party agreement
The US is in ITU Region 2
A station under automatic control still has a responsible licensee

G2A.note: Convention on HF is lower sideband below 10 MHz and upper sideband above it, with the exceptions of 60 m and all the VHF/UHF SSB bands, which use USB. To break into a contact on phone say your call sign between transmissions — not 'break', which signals an emergency in many nets.
key_facts: LSB on 160, 80 and 40 m; USB on 20 m and above
60 m uses USB regardless of the below-10-MHz rule
Say your call sign to join a contact, not 'break'
Excessive mic gain or speech processing causes splatter

G2B.note: Operating well is mostly courtesy plus awareness of what else is on the band. Listen before transmitting, use the minimum power, and respect band plans and the calling frequencies. During an emergency net, stay off the frequency unless you can help. A station in distress has absolute priority.
key_facts: Always listen before transmitting on a frequency
Use the minimum power necessary
Band plans are voluntary agreements, not FCC rules
Emergency traffic takes precedence over everything else

G2C.note: CW procedure is compact by design. Q signals compress common phrases: QRM is interference from other stations, QRN is atmospheric noise, QSY means change frequency, QRZ asks who is calling. Full break-in, or QSK, lets you hear between your own dits — useful for catching a station breaking in mid-transmission.
key_facts: QRM = interference from stations, QRN = atmospheric noise
QSY = change frequency, QRZ = who is calling me, QRS = send slower
Full break-in (QSK) receives between the elements of your own sending
Answer a CQ at or slightly below the sender's speed

G2D.note: The Volunteer Monitor Program is the ARRL-administered successor to the Official Observer scheme; volunteers monitor the bands and report both good practice and rule violations to the FCC. Beyond that, this group covers routine HF habits — logging, QSLing, and working DX politely.
key_facts: The Volunteer Monitor Program is administered by the ARRL under FCC agreement
Volunteer Monitors report violations and also good operating
Logging is no longer required by the FCC but remains good practice
When working a DX pileup, listen first to learn the DX station's pattern

G3A.note: The sun drives HF. Solar flux and sunspot number track how much ionising radiation is reaching the ionosphere: more flux means a denser F layer and higher usable frequencies. The A and K indices measure geomagnetic disturbance instead — and disturbance is bad news, causing absorption and wrecking polar paths.
key_facts: Higher solar flux raises the MUF and opens the higher bands
K index: 0-9, updated every 3 hours. A index: daily, linear
Low A and K means a quiet, stable geomagnetic field
A coronal mass ejection can cause a geomagnetic storm 20-40 hours later

G3B.note: The MUF is the highest frequency that will still refract back to earth on a given path; the LUF is the lowest that will get through D-layer absorption. Work between them, and near the MUF for best results. Long path goes the other way round the earth — 180 degrees from short path and much further.
key_facts: Work below the MUF and above the LUF
The best band is usually just below the MUF
Long path is 180 degrees from short path and about 40,000 km minus the short path
Raising the frequency above the MUF means the signal passes into space

G3C.note: The ionosphere is layered. The D region absorbs low frequencies by day and vanishes at night, which is why 160 and 80 m come alive after dark. E is intermittent. F splits into F1 and F2 by day and merges at night; F2 does the long-haul work. Send a signal above the critical frequency straight up and it escapes.
key_facts: D layer absorbs, mostly below 10 MHz, and disappears at night
F2 is the highest layer and supports the longest hops
Critical frequency is the highest that returns at vertical incidence
NVIS uses high-angle radiation below foF2 for regional coverage with no skip zone

G4A.note: Station configuration, and the controls that shape a signal. A notch filter removes a single interfering carrier. Attenuators protect the front end from very strong signals. The transmit bandwidth control on a modern rig sets how wide your SSB signal is, and an ALC meter shows whether you are driving an amplifier correctly.
key_facts: A notch filter removes a single unwanted carrier
ALC prevents overdriving; watch it when driving an amplifier
An attenuator reduces very strong signals to prevent overload
IF shift moves the passband without moving the received frequency

G4B.note: Choose the instrument for the measurement. An oscilloscope shows a waveform against time, which is how you spot flat-topping. A spectrum analyser shows amplitude against frequency, which is how you spot harmonics and splatter. A dummy load lets you test at full power without radiating.
key_facts: Oscilloscope: amplitude versus time. Spectrum analyser: amplitude versus frequency
A dummy load is a non-radiating 50-ohm resistive load
A voltmeter's high input impedance avoids loading the circuit under test
Directional wattmeters read forward and reflected power separately

G4C.note: Interference cures come in two halves: stop your station radiating what it should not, and stop the affected device receiving what it should not. Harmonics from the transmitter are your problem and need filtering at the transmitter. Fundamental overload of a neighbour's device is their equipment failing to reject a legal signal.
key_facts: A low-pass filter at the transmitter cuts harmonic radiation
A high-pass filter at the affected receiver cuts fundamental overload
Ferrite chokes on cables break up common-mode currents
Bond all station equipment to a single ground point to avoid ground loops

G4D.note: A speech processor raises average power by compressing the audio, which improves readability on a weak SSB signal — but overdone it distorts and splatters. S meters are only roughly standardised: S9 is defined as 50 microvolts at the antenna on HF, and each S unit is nominally 6 dB.
key_facts: S9 = 50 microvolts at the receiver input on HF
One S unit is approximately 6 dB
A speech processor raises average talk power, not peak power
Leave about 3 kHz clearance from a band edge when operating SSB

G4E.note: Mobile and portable stations live with limited power and compromise antennas. A short mobile whip needs a loading coil to be resonant, and most of its loss is in ground and coil resistance — a larger coil and a capacity hat help. Alternative power sources have their own problems: solar charge controllers and switching supplies both make RF noise.
key_facts: A loading coil resonates a physically short mobile antenna
Connect a mobile transceiver directly to the battery with fused leads
Alternator whine enters through the DC power leads
A properly sized solar panel needs a charge controller to protect the battery

G5A.note: Reactance is frequency-dependent opposition: inductive reactance rises with frequency, capacitive reactance falls. At resonance they are equal and cancel, leaving pure resistance — this is what makes tuned circuits and resonant antennas work. Impedance transformation lets you match one impedance to another, which is what a transformer or a matching network does.
key_facts: X_L = 2 x pi x f x L, rising with frequency
X_C = 1 / (2 x pi x f x C), falling with frequency
At resonance X_L = X_C and the impedance is purely resistive
A quarter-wave matching section uses Z = square root of (Zin x Zout)

G5B.note: The decibel and the basic power arithmetic. Remember 3 dB as double and 10 dB as ten times and most exam questions fall out. RMS is the DC-equivalent value of a sine wave — the value that produces the same heating — and it is peak divided by the square root of two. PEP is what the FCC limit is measured in.
key_facts: dB = 10 x log10(power ratio); 3 dB doubles, 10 dB is ten times
RMS = peak x 0.707;  peak = RMS x 1.414
Peak-to-peak is twice the peak value
PEP = RMS voltage squared, divided by load resistance, for a single tone

G5C.note: Series and parallel behave oppositely for resistors and capacitors. Resistors and inductors add in series; capacitors add in parallel. A transformer's voltage ratio follows its turns ratio, and its impedance ratio follows the square of the turns ratio — that squared relationship is the one most often missed.
key_facts: Resistors and inductors: add in series, reciprocal sum in parallel
Capacitors: add in parallel, reciprocal sum in series
Transformer voltage ratio = turns ratio
Transformer impedance ratio = turns ratio squared

G6A.note: Component behaviour beyond the ideal. Every real component has parasitics: a capacitor has lead inductance, a resistor has capacitance, and both matter at RF. Electrolytic capacitors are polarised and fail if reversed. Diodes have a forward voltage drop — about 0.7 V for silicon, 0.3 V for germanium.
key_facts: Silicon diode drops about 0.7 V forward; germanium about 0.3 V
Electrolytic capacitors are polarised and must be fitted the right way round
Wire-wound resistors are inductive and unsuitable at RF
A Zener diode regulates by conducting in reverse at a set voltage

G6B.note: Integrated circuits and the small parts around them. An MMIC is a monolithic microwave amplifier in a tiny package needing few external parts. Ferrite beads and toroids suppress or transform RF depending on the material's permeability. Choose connectors by frequency: type N above 400 MHz, BNC for low-power VHF.
key_facts: An MMIC is a monolithic microwave integrated circuit amplifier
Ferrite mix determines whether a core suppresses or transforms
Type N connectors are preferred above 400 MHz
An LED is a diode that emits light when forward biased

G7A.note: A linear power supply rectifies, filters and regulates. A full-wave bridge uses four diodes and produces a ripple at twice the mains frequency, which is easier to filter than a half-wave rectifier's. The filter capacitor smooths the pulsating DC; a bleeder resistor discharges it safely when the supply is switched off.
key_facts: Full-wave bridge: four diodes, ripple at twice mains frequency
Half-wave: one diode, ripple at mains frequency, harder to filter
A larger filter capacitor reduces ripple
A bleeder resistor discharges filter capacitors for safety

G7B.note: Amplifier class describes how much of the input cycle the device conducts for. Class A conducts the whole cycle — most linear, least efficient. Class C conducts less than half and is efficient but badly distorting, so it suits FM and CW but never SSB. An oscillator is an amplifier with positive feedback and a frequency-determining network.
key_facts: Class A: conducts 360 degrees, most linear, least efficient
Class C: conducts under 180 degrees, efficient, non-linear
SSB needs a linear amplifier: class A or AB
An oscillator needs gain, positive feedback and a tuned circuit

G7C.note: A superheterodyne mixes the incoming signal with a local oscillator to a fixed intermediate frequency, where good filters are practical. Filter bandwidth is chosen to match the mode: narrow for CW, about 2.4 kHz for SSB. DSP does the same filtering in software, and can also implement noise reduction and automatic notching.
key_facts: A mixer produces the sum and difference of its two inputs
Roofing filters protect the IF stages from strong nearby signals
Choose about 500 Hz for CW, 2.4 kHz for SSB, 6 kHz for AM
DSP filtering is done numerically after the signal is digitised

G8A.note: Modulation methods and their consequences. AM has a carrier and two sidebands; SSB throws away the carrier and one sideband, saving both power and spectrum. FM varies frequency rather than amplitude, so it is immune to amplitude noise but needs more bandwidth. Overmodulation on any mode produces splatter that lands on your neighbours.
key_facts: AM bandwidth is twice the highest audio frequency
SSB puts all transmitter power into one sideband
Overmodulation causes splatter and distortion
The modulation envelope is the shape of the RF amplitude over time

G8B.note: Frequency changing and the bandwidth consequences. Mixing two signals produces the sum and the difference, which is how a transmitter reaches its output frequency. Deviation sets FM bandwidth: Carson's rule says bandwidth is roughly twice the sum of deviation and highest audio frequency. Intermodulation arises when two signals mix in a non-linear stage.
key_facts: A mixer output contains the sum and difference frequencies
Carson's rule: bandwidth ~ 2 x (deviation + highest modulating frequency)
Intermodulation products come from non-linearity, often in an overloaded stage
Third-order products fall closest to the wanted signals and are hardest to filter

G8C.note: Digital emissions differ in bandwidth, speed and robustness. FT8 is extremely narrow and works far below the noise, at the cost of tiny fixed messages. PSK31 is a conversational keyboard mode. FSK and its relatives shift between tones. Packet and its descendants add addressing and error checking, and can be relayed.
key_facts: FT8 uses 15-second transmit slots and works below the noise floor
PSK31 is about 31 Hz wide
Baud is symbols per second, not bits per second
An ARQ protocol requests retransmission of frames received in error

G9A.note: Characteristic impedance is set by the geometry of the line, not its length. SWR is the ratio of the impedances when they mismatch — a 100-ohm load on 50-ohm line gives 2:1, and so does a 25-ohm load. Loss in the line converts reflected power to heat, which is why a high SWR on a long lossy run costs so much.
key_facts: SWR = higher impedance divided by lower, for a resistive load
Characteristic impedance depends on conductor size and spacing, not length
Feed line loss rises with frequency and with SWR
A matched line has SWR 1:1 and no reflected power

G9B.note: The half-wave dipole is the reference antenna. Fed at the centre it presents roughly 70 ohms, radiates broadside to the wire, and its length is about 468 divided by frequency in MHz, in feet. Height above ground dominates its radiation angle: low means high-angle and short-range, high means low-angle and DX.
key_facts: Half-wave dipole in feet = 468 / f(MHz)
Centre-fed dipole feed point impedance is about 70 ohms
A quarter-wave vertical needs a ground plane or radials
A dipole low over ground radiates at a high angle — good for NVIS

G9C.note: A Yagi concentrates radiation by adding parasitic elements: a reflector behind, slightly longer, and one or more directors in front, slightly shorter. Gain rises with boom length, and beamwidth narrows as gain rises. Front-to-back ratio measures how well it rejects signals from behind — useful for nulling interference.
key_facts: Reflector is longer than the driven element; directors are shorter
More elements and longer boom means more gain, narrower beamwidth
Front-to-back ratio measures rejection off the rear
Stacking two antennas vertically lowers the radiation angle

G9D.note: Special-purpose antennas. A random wire against a good ground needs a tuner and works many bands at the cost of RF in the shack. A NVIS antenna is a low horizontal wire for regional work. A Beverage is a very long, low receiving wire that is quiet and directional but very inefficient — receive only.
key_facts: A Beverage is a long, low receiving antenna, poor for transmitting
NVIS uses a low horizontal antenna for high-angle regional coverage
A trap antenna uses resonant traps to work several bands
Loop antennas can null an interfering signal by rotation

G0A.note: RF exposure evaluation is required of every station. The limits depend on frequency, on whether the exposure is controlled or uncontrolled, and on duty cycle and averaging time. Uncontrolled limits are stricter and apply to neighbours and passers-by. Raising the antenna and increasing separation are the most effective fixes.
key_facts: Every amateur station must perform a routine RF exposure evaluation
Uncontrolled exposure limits are lower than controlled limits
Averaging time is 6 minutes controlled, 30 minutes uncontrolled
Duty cycle and antenna gain both enter the calculation

G0B.note: Station wiring and mechanical safety. Size conductors and fuses for the current, fuse the ungrounded conductor, and bond equipment to a single point ground so no fault current flows through a signal cable. Interlocks keep amplifier cabinets safe. On the tower, never climb alone, and keep clear of power lines.
key_facts: Fuse the hot conductor; ground the chassis of every unit
Bond all station equipment to a single point ground
Use conductors sized for the current, not for convenience
An interlock removes high voltage when a cabinet is opened

G2E.note: Digital operating on HF has its own etiquette and settings. Most modes are worked in upper sideband regardless of band, because the software cares about audio tone frequencies rather than the sideband convention. Keep drive low enough that ALC barely moves — overdriving a digital signal spreads it across the band and is the commonest fault.
key_facts: Most HF digital modes use USB on every band
Set audio drive so ALC action is minimal; overdrive causes splatter
FT8 transmits in 15-second slots synchronised to the clock
Your PC clock must be accurate within about a second for FT8/JS8
A waterfall display shows signals across the passband over time
